question: A 50-year-old man presents with a complaint of pain and swelling of his right leg for the past 2 days. He remembers hitting his leg against a table 3 days earlier. Since then, the pain and swelling of the leg have gradually increased. His past medical history is significant for atopy and pulmonary tuberculosis. The patient reports a 20-pack-year smoking history and currently smokes 2 packs of cigarettes per day. His pulse is 98/min, respiratory rate is 15/min, temperature is 38.4°C (101.2°F), and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. On physical examination, his right leg is visibly swollen up to the groin with moderate erythema and 2+ pitting edema. The peripheral pulses are 2+ in the right leg and there is no discomfort. There is no increased resistance or pain in the right calf in response to forced dorsiflexion of the right foot. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Trauma to the right leg -> pain and swelling -> gradual increase in symptoms -> significant swelling and erythema up to the groin -> 80% CHAIN: Trauma to the right leg -> possible deep vein thrombosis (DVT) -> 2+ pitting edema -> 2+ peripheral pulses -> no discomfort with forced dorsiflexion -> 70% CHAIN: Trauma to the right leg -> possible compartment syndrome -> no increased resistance or pain with forced dorsiflexion -> 60% CHAIN: Trauma to the right leg -> possible cellulitis -> moderate erythema -> 50% CHAIN: Trauma to the right leg -> possible muscle contusion -> 80%
enhanced_information: The patient's presentation with pain, swelling, and erythema in the right leg following trauma raises concern for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Given the absence of discomfort with forced dorsiflexion and 2+ peripheral pulses, DVT is more likely than compartment syndrome. The best next step in management would be to perform an ultrasound of the right leg to confirm the presence of DVT.
